candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 33 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 34 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 35 the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but 36 not required. 37

candidates.statement: For a drug product to be approved by FDA, a sponsor must provide substantial evidence 6 , 7 that 57 the drug has the effect it purports to have under the conditions of use described in the proposed 58 labeling and that the drug’s benefits outweigh its risks. Generally, the evidence is derived from 59 adequate and well-controlled clinical studies. Human challenge studies (i.e., exposing volunteers 60 to acute, high doses of ionizing radiation to study the effects of the drug) are not ethical and field 61 trials are not feasible when developing drugs for ARS. Under such circumstances, FDA may 62 grant approval under the Animal Rule, based on adequate and well-controlled animal efficacy 63 studies, when the results of those studies establish that the drug is reasonably likely to produce 64 clinical benefit in humans. However, it is important to note that under the Animal Rule, human 65 studies are still required to demonstrate a drug’s safety. 8

candidates.context: Improving capabilities for addressing radiological and nuclear emergencies is a national 76 priority. 9 FDA has developed distinct approaches to facilitate and expedite development and 77 review of new drugs to address unmet medical needs for treating serious or life-threatening 78 conditions. 10 Drugs developed for ARS may be eligible for certain FDA expedited programs 79 (e.g., fast track and priority review) or other FDA programs (e.g., orphan drug designation). 11 Drugs being developed under the Animal Rule might meet the statutory requirement for 84 breakthrough therapy designation when there is such preliminary clinical evidence in a condition 85 closely related to the indication sought under the Animal Rule. For example, clinical evidence in 86 chemotherapy-induced myelosuppression might support breakthrough therapy designation for 87 ARS-associated myelosuppression. 88

candidates.statement: Developing the animal models in which to test the efficacy of investigational products being 90 developed under the Animal Rule is challenging. Animal models should reflect the clinical 91 condition for which the drug is being developed (e.g., H-ARS or GI-ARS). The Animal Rule 92 guidance defines animal model as “a specific combination of an animal species, challenge agent, 93 and route of exposure that produces a disease process or pathological condition that in multiple 94 important aspects corresponds to the human disease or condition of interest.” 14 Given the 95 multisystem nature of ARS, radiation exposure directed at sections of the body (e.g., thoracic or 96 abdominal region) may be of limited value for confirmatory studies. candidates.statement: Design considerations for animal efficacy studies would be different for a drug for prophylaxis 136 compared with a drug for treatment. Pre-exposure prophylaxis studies should be designed to 137 determine the likely time course of the prophylactic effect (i.e., the minimum time the subject 138 must wait after taking the drug before radiation exposure) and how long the prophylactic effect 139 lasts. Study design should also incorporate standard of care for postradiation exposure treatment, 140 including the potential concurrent use of LGFs, for example. 141

candidates.statement: For selection of a human dose based on a PD marker, the PD marker should be shown in animals 180 and humans to correlate with the mechanism of action by which the drug prevents or 181 substantially reduces the radiation-induced condition and with the desired clinical outcome (i.e., 182 enhancement of survival or prevention of major morbidity). In addition, human PK/PD studies 183 should support a human drug dose that would result in PD marker levels in the desired range that 184 is predictive of marker levels associated with efficacy in the adequate and well-controlled animal 185 studies. The PD marker and its assay methods and performance characteristics in the animal 186 species and in humans should be described and agreed upon with FDA. 187

candidates.statement: Under the Animal Rule, the nonclinical studies needed to support human safety trials are the 227 same as those required under traditional drug development with the expectation that nonclinical 228 safety and toxicity studies generally should be conducted under good laboratory practice (GLP) 229 regulations (21 CFR part 58). 25

candidates.statement: A sufficiently characterized drug is critical to relate the drug used in Animal Rule–specific 249 nonclinical studies to the drug proposed for use in human studies. Sponsors should perform the 250 adequate and well-controlled animal efficacy studies intended to support approval and human 251 safety studies using the to-be-marketed drug formulation. Any differences between the 252 formulation used and the to-be-marketed formulation should be discussed with the review 253 division before studies are initiated. If the animal model used makes dosing with the to-be- 254 marketed human drug formulation difficult, sponsors should administer the drug to the animals 255 using a dosing regimen that would provide drug exposures comparable to those in humans. 256

candidates.statement: Drugs, as defined under section 201(g) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C 263 Act), contain active ingredients and may contain inactive ingredients. As such, study drug 264 ingredients are required to be produced at facilities that comply with current good manufacturing 265 practice (CGMP) requirements under section 501(a)(2)(B) of the FD&C Act. 28 When an IND is 266 submitted, regulations under 21 CFR 312.23(a)(7) require including the CMC section in the IND 267 describing the composition, manufacture, and control of the drug substance and the drug product. 268 This information is necessary to ensure the proper identification, quality, purity, and strength of 269 the investigational drug. The amount of information needed to make that assurance will vary 270 with the phase of the investigation, the proposed formulation, and duration of the investigation. 29

The metric of biological 297 effect (e.g., LD50/60, or lethal dose sufficient to kill 50 percent of irradiated animals within 60 298 days) can be attained through controlled irradiation conditions irrespective of radiation source or 299 radiation type. Sponsors should provide a detailed justification for the source and type of 300 radiation, the dose or doses to be used in a study, how the animals would be irradiated, and the 301 relevance to the intended clinical conditions of use. A determination of dose modification factor 302 (i.e., a demonstration that the mortality caused by various radiation doses in treated animals can 303 be matched at any level of radiation by a constant fraction of the radiation dose in untreated 304 animals) is not required. For the adequate and well-controlled animal efficacy studies, FDA 305 generally considers demonstration of efficacy against the effects of a single dose level of 306 radiation to be sufficient (e.g., animals exposed to a single dose of 10 Gy); however, there may 307 be circumstances for which FDA would recommend that a sponsor test its investigational drug 308 against the effects of a range of dose levels of radiation (e.g., animals exposed to a single dose of 309 7.0, 8.5, or 10 Gy). 310

candidates.statement: It is important to ensure the humane care and use of the laboratory animals to minimize distress 343 and pain and to provide nutritional and fluid support. Supportive care, as defined in the Animal 344 Rule guidance, “is needed only to mimic, to the extent possible, the human clinical scenario.” If 345 the expected clinical scenario is to use the drug in a mass-casualty situation in which supportive 346 care is not immediately available, the adequate and well-controlled animal efficacy studies 347 necessary for approval may be conducted with adequate veterinary care necessary to minimize 348 pain and suffering. Alternatively, if the expected clinical setting is to use the drug in a situation 349 in which supportive care is available, FDA recommends that sponsors propose and justify a 350 supportive care regimen that will mimic the proposed use of the product. Sponsors should 351 discuss all animal care interventions with the review division. 34
candidates.context: When a drug is pharmacologically active only in humans and is intended to address an unmet 337 medical need for ARS, the use of a surrogate drug that achieves the engagement of the 338 pharmacological target in animals may be considered for the animal efficacy studies. In such 339 circumstances, it is strongly recommended that sponsors meet with the review division to 340 determine the adequacy of a surrogate drug for the adequate and well-controlled efficacy studies. 341 E. Efficacy Endpoints 354

candidates.statement: Generally, enhancing survival or preventing major morbidity should be the primary endpoint in 373 animal efficacy studies. 35 In addition to improved survival, endpoints reflecting reduction in 374 important ARS complications or prevention of major morbidity, such as fewer major 375 hemorrhages, needed transfusions, or serious infections, may also be acceptable as primary 376 efficacy outcomes. For a survival benefit, overall survival at a relevant time point (e.g., when 377 the proportion of animals surviving has plateaued), rather than only reduction in time to death 378 without any difference in the proportion of animals that ultimately survive, should be 379 demonstrated. The timing of assessing the primary endpoint should be based upon natural 380 history studies. Typically, survival should be evaluated for 30 days for rodents and 60 days for 381 nonrodents, given that their Kaplan-Meier survival curves after radiation exposure plateau at 382 these time points in these animals. PD endpoints, such as a favorable effect on neutropenia in an 383 efficacy study of an LGF, are useful in supporting the mechanism of action of the drug and for 384 selecting an effective dose and regimen in humans and are considered secondary efficacy 385 endpoints. Sponsors are strongly encouraged to discuss potential efficacy endpoints in animal 386 studies with the review division before starting the study. 387
candidates.context: For each of the drugs approved for H-ARS to date (i.e., LGFs: filgrastim, pegfilgrastim, and 362 sargramostim; and thrombopoietin receptor agonist: romiplostim), a single animal efficacy study 363 in a single NHP model of H-ARS was required to provide substantial evidence of effectiveness, 364 estimate the treatment effect, and establish a dose and regimen for humans. The adequate and 365 well-controlled animal efficacy studies demonstrated an increase in survival at a prespecified 366 time point posttreatment (the prospectively defined primary endpoint) accompanied by the 367 supportive evidence of the expected pharmacological effect (i.e., resolution of neutropenia or 368 thrombocytopenia); therefore, the studies were relied on for approval. For each of the drugs 369 discussed, the results of the adequate and well-controlled efficacy study were supported by 370 existing human efficacy

candidates.statement: GI-ARS generally occurs after exposure to a much greater radiation dose than H-ARS (e.g., 389 LD50/15 of 11.33 Gy for GI-ARS versus LD50/60 of 7.54 Gy for H-ARS in NHP total-body 390 irradiation models). 36 Therefore, even when GI-ARS is the intended target for therapy, the 391 animal models and the efficacy outcomes should consider the manifestations of H-ARS. For 392 example, improvement in survival at 10 to 15 days in an animal model of GI-ARS will provide 393 useful information on a drug’s activity in exploratory, proof-of-concept studies before lethality 394 attributable to H-ARS ensues. To provide substantial evidence of effectiveness of an 395 investigational drug for the treatment of GI-ARS, it is important to study the effect of the drug on 396 overall survival and safety assessed at a time point defined by natural history studies of radiation 397 doses that induce GI-ARS (e.g., 30 and 60 days, respectively, in rodents and NHPs). candidates.statement: Certain investigational drugs under development for treating ARS might be associated with 408 severe adverse reactions that preclude a full characterization of the drug’s safety in healthy adult 409 volunteers. The Agency will not rely primarily on nonclinical information to assess safety; 410 approval of a new drug requires an adequate human safety database, regardless of the regulatory 411 development pathway. 37 , 38 If nonclinical or clinical data raise safety concerns about further 412 testing of the investigational drug in healthy adult volunteers, sponsors should consider acquiring 413 the needed human safety information in a patient population for which the drug offers a potential 414 benefit that justifies the drug’s risks. Human safety data from a drug development program for 415 which the drug’s benefit-risk is appropriate could then be used to support the ARS indication. 416 Sponsors should provide a justification for extrapolating to ARS the human safety data from the 417 clinical condition chosen. 418
candidates.context: F. Clinical Safety Studies 406 Because approval of drugs under the Animal Rule also requires an adequate human safety 420 database, clinical safety data from previous clinical experience may be applicable. For example, 421 the safety of certain LGFs for use in H-ARS was extrapolated from the previously approved 422 clinical uses in oncology indications. 423
